Customising MixMustR Stan code

Diego Barneche

2026-10-22

Source: vignettes/custom-stan-code.Rmd
custom-stan-code.Rmd

Overview

By default, run_mixmustr_models() calls build_stancode() internally, so the Stan program for each model variant is (re)generated and written to model_choices$code_path every time models are run. This is convenient, but it also means that any manual edits to those .stan files would be overwritten.

Advanced users may want to change parts of the Stan program, for example to use more informative priors that reflect expert knowledge. This vignette illustrates a workflow to do so:

  1. Generate the standard Stan program with build_stancode().
  2. Edit the Stan code (here, two priors).
  3. Fit the edited model with run_mixmustr_models(..., build_code = FALSE), which skips build_stancode() and uses the .stan file as is.

We assume familiarity with the Introduction to MixMustR vignette.

library(MixMustR)
rstan::rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)
options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())

Step 1: Choose a model variant and generate its Stan code

We use the variant with fixed sampled-source signatures, a fixed unsampled-source signature, and independent observations (row 6 of mixmustr_models), which is the quickest to fit.

model_choice <- mixmustr_models[6, ]
model_choice
#>   sample_tracer fix_unsampled hierarchical
#> 6         FALSE          TRUE        FALSE
#>                                                             code_path
#> 6 stan/sample_tracer_FALSE_fix_unsampled_TRUE_hierarchical_FALSE.stan

Rather than using the default code_path, we point it to a new file so that the customised program is kept separate from the standard ones. Note that the file name (without extension) is also used as the Stan model name and as the name of the corresponding element in the output of run_mixmustr_models(). Here we use a temporary directory; in a real analysis you would typically use a folder within your project.

stan_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "mixmustr_stan")
dir.create(stan_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)
model_choice$code_path <- file.path(stan_dir, "custom_priors.stan")

Now generate the standard Stan program for this variant and write it to disk:

build_stancode(
  sample_tracer = model_choice$sample_tracer,
  fix_unsampled = model_choice$fix_unsampled,
  hierarchical = model_choice$hierarchical,
  code_path = model_choice$code_path
) |>
  invisible()
file.exists(model_choice$code_path)
#> [1] TRUE

The priors live in the model block. Let’s print them:

stan_code <- readLines(model_choice$code_path)
model_start <- grep("^model \\{", stan_code)
prior_lines <- grep(" ~ ", stan_code)
prior_lines <- prior_lines[prior_lines > model_start]
cat(stan_code[prior_lines], sep = "\n")
#>   to_vector(z_raw) ~ std_normal();
#>   sigma_z ~ normal(0, 1);
#>   beta0 ~ normal(0, 1.5);
#>   log_sigma_y_raw ~ normal(0, 0.5);
#>   nu_rho ~ gamma(2, 0.1);
#>       ln_rho[n, j] ~ student_t(nu_rho, log_p_n[j], sigma_ln_rho[n, j]);
#>     Y[n] ~ normal(mu_n, sigma_n);

The last two lines are the stream-2 and stream-1 likelihoods; the remaining ones are priors. For this variant:

  • beta0 are the baseline logits of each sampled source relative to the unsampled source (the reference category).
  • sigma_z are the observation-level standard deviations of those logits.
  • log_sigma_y_raw controls the residual tracer scale for data stream 1.
  • nu_rho are the degrees of freedom of the Student-t likelihood for data stream 2.

Step 2: Modify the Stan code

Suppose prior knowledge suggests that the mixing proportions of sampled sources are unlikely to be very extreme relative to the unsampled source, and that observation-level departures from those baseline logits should be small. We tighten the prior on beta0 and replace the half-normal prior on sigma_z with an exponential prior.

The .stan file can be edited in any text editor. Here we do it programmatically, checking that each line to be replaced is present exactly once:

replacements <- c(
  "  beta0 ~ normal(0, 1.5);" = "  beta0 ~ normal(0, 1); // modified prior",
  "  sigma_z ~ normal(0, 1);" = "  sigma_z ~ exponential(2); // modified prior"
)
for (old in names(replacements)) {
  stopifnot(sum(stan_code == old) == 1)
  stan_code[stan_code == old] <- replacements[[old]]
}
writeLines(stan_code, model_choice$code_path)

It is good practice to check that the edited program still parses before fitting it:

rstan::stanc(file = model_choice$code_path)$status
#> [1] TRUE

When editing the Stan code, keep in mind that:

  • The data block must remain compatible with the data list produced by mixmustr_wrangle_input(). The sample_tracer, fix_unsampled, and hierarchical columns in model_choice must therefore match the variant the file was generated from.
  • The post-processing functions (e.g., make_post_prop_long() and mixmustr_bayes_R2()) rely on the mixing-proportion matrix p, so it should not be renamed or removed.
  • Tracer observations and source signatures are standardised by mixmustr_wrangle_input() before fitting, so priors on tracer-scale quantities apply on the standardised scale.

Step 3: Fit the modified model

We now call run_mixmustr_models() with build_code = FALSE. This skips build_stancode() so the edited file is not overwritten. If the file at code_path did not exist, run_mixmustr_models() would stop with an informative error.

model_fits <- run_mixmustr_models(
  model_choice, synthetic_df_convergent, tracer_parameters,
  sigma_ln_rho = 1, build_code = FALSE, iter = 2e3, warmup = 1e3,
  chains = 4, cores = 4
)

The output is named after the .stan file. We can confirm that the fitted model used the modified priors:

names(model_fits)
#> [1] "custom_priors"
fit <- model_fits$custom_priors$model
fitted_code <- strsplit(rstan::get_stancode(fit), "\n")[[1]]
cat(grep("modified prior", fitted_code, value = TRUE), sep = "\n")
#>   sigma_z ~ exponential(2); // modified prior
#>   beta0 ~ normal(0, 1); // modified prior

And inspect the parameters whose priors were changed:

print(fit, pars = c("beta0", "sigma_z"), probs = c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))
#> Inference for Stan model: custom_priors.
#> 4 chains, each with iter=2000; warmup=1000; thin=1; 
#> post-warmup draws per chain=1000, total post-warmup draws=4000.
#> 
#>             mean se_mean   sd  2.5%   50% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
#> beta0[1]    0.17    0.01 0.20 -0.23  0.18  0.54  1304 1.00
#> beta0[2]   -1.10    0.01 0.26 -1.61 -1.09 -0.61  1337 1.00
#> beta0[3]   -1.79    0.00 0.18 -2.16 -1.79 -1.45  2241 1.00
#> beta0[4]   -0.77    0.01 0.28 -1.33 -0.78 -0.23  1054 1.00
#> beta0[5]   -0.43    0.01 0.34 -1.09 -0.43  0.24   637 1.00
#> beta0[6]   -0.39    0.01 0.21 -0.78 -0.39  0.01  1568 1.00
#> sigma_z[1]  1.20    0.01 0.17  0.91  1.19  1.55   823 1.00
#> sigma_z[2]  2.07    0.00 0.18  1.75  2.06  2.46  1546 1.00
#> sigma_z[3]  0.50    0.01 0.27  0.03  0.50  1.00   471 1.01
#> sigma_z[4]  2.32    0.01 0.24  1.87  2.31  2.81  1103 1.00
#> sigma_z[5]  3.11    0.01 0.24  2.66  3.10  3.61   903 1.00
#> sigma_z[6]  1.38    0.00 0.16  1.08  1.37  1.70  1094 1.00

#> Samples were drawn using NUTS(diag_e) at Thu Oct 22 12:57:48 2026.

#> convergence, Rhat=1).

The fitted model can be used with all MixMustR post-processing tools, as usual:

library(ggplot2)
make_post_prop_long(
  fit, tracer_parameters$mus, synthetic_df_convergent, target = "df_stream_2",
  n = 1
) |>
  plot_multiple_faceted_scatter_avg() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(
    y = "Observed (simulated) from composition data (data stream 2)",
    title = "Model fit performance mixing proportions",
    subtitle = "Custom priors on beta0 and sigma_z"
  )

mixmustr_bayes_R2(
  fit, summary = TRUE, data_streams_list = synthetic_df_convergent,
  target = "df_stream_2", order_ref = tracer_parameters$mus$source
)
#>              Source mean 2.5%HDI 97.5%HDI
#> 1        Macroalgae 0.80    0.77     0.84
#> 2          Mangrove 0.93    0.90     0.96
#> 3         Saltmarsh 0.11    0.03     0.24
#> 4          Seagrass 0.81    0.75     0.87
#> 5              SPOM 0.90    0.89     0.92
#> 6 Terrestrial grass 0.85    0.79     0.90
#> 7         Unsampled 0.33    0.27     0.40

Recap

  1. Use build_stancode() with a custom code_path to generate the standard Stan program for the chosen variant.
  2. Edit the .stan file (e.g., priors), keeping the data block and the mixing-proportion matrix p intact.
  3. Fit with run_mixmustr_models(..., build_code = FALSE) so the edited file is used as is.
